draft.title: Derivatives of inverse circular functions
card: The derivative of arcsin(x) is 1/√(1 − x²), for −1 < x < 1.
The derivative of arctan(x) is 1/(1 + x²), for all real x.
When the input is a function u of x, use the chain rule. The derivative of arctan(u) is u′/(1 + u²).
Example: for y = arctan(3x), u = 3x and u′ = 3. So dy/dx = 3/(1 + 9x²).
draft.remember: Arcsin gives 1/√(1 − x²), arctan gives 1/(1 + x²), and the chain rule adds u′.

a.q: What is the derivative of arcsin(x)?
a.why: The derivative of arcsin(x) is 1/√(1 − x²). The option 1/(1 + x²) is the derivative of arctan(x), a neighbouring result.
a.clue: The answer has a square root in the denominator.

b.q: What is dy/dx when y = arctan(2x) at x = 1/2?
b.why: By the chain rule, dy/dx = 2/(1 + 4x²). At x = 1/2, 4x² = 1, so dy/dx = 2/2 = 1. The option 2 leaves out the 1 + 4x² in the denominator.
b.clue: Let u = 2x and multiply by u′ = 2.

problems.detail: "the chain rule adds u′" could be read as adding u′. The chain rule multiplies by u′ (u′/(1 + u²)), so it should say "multiplies by u′" or "puts u′ on top".

check.summary: Both questions have exactly one correct answer, and the facts and explanations check out. The only problem is the remember line, which says the chain rule "adds u′" when it multiplies by u′.

final.title: Derivatives of inverse circular functions
card: The derivative of \(\arcsin(x)\) is \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - x^{2}}}\), for \(-1 < x < 1\).
The derivative of \(\arctan(x)\) is \(\frac{1}{1 + x^{2}}\), for all real \(x\).
When the input is a function \(u\) of \(x\), use the chain rule. The derivative of \(\arctan(u)\) is \(\frac{u'}{1 + u^{2}}\).
final.remember: \(\arcsin\) gives \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - x^{2}}}\), \(\arctan\) gives \(\frac{1}{1 + x^{2}}\), and the chain rule puts \(u'\) on top.

a.why: The derivative of \(\arcsin(x)\) is \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - x^{2}}}\). The option \(\frac{1}{1 + x^{2}}\) is the derivative of \(\arctan(x)\), a neighbouring result.
a.clue: The answer has a square root in the denominator.

b.why: By the chain rule, \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{2}{1 + 4x^{2}}\). At \(x = \frac{1}{2}\), \(4x^{2} = 1\), so \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{2}{2} = 1\). The option \(\frac{1}{2}\) forgets to multiply by \(u' = 2\).
